los.text: Describe the main causes and signs and symptoms of common male urological diseases
los.html:
ConditionCauses / riskSigns & symptoms
BPHAge, androgens (DHT)LUTS: hesitancy, weak stream, terminal dribbling, frequency, nocturia, urgency; smooth enlarged prostate on DRE; retention
Prostate cancerAge, Black ethnicity, FHx, BRCA2Often asymptomatic; LUTS, haematuria, bone pain (metastases), hard irregular prostate
ProstatitisAcute: E. coli/gram-negatives; chronic pelvic pain syndromeFever, perineal pain, dysuria, very tender prostate
Urinary retentionAcute: BPH + trigger (anticholinergics, constipation, alcohol, surgery); chronic: BPHAcute: painful, can't pass urine, palpable bladder; chronic: painless, overflow incontinence, ± renal impairment
Testicular torsionBell-clapper deformity, adolescentsSudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex, vomiting
Epididymo-orchitis<35: chlamydia/gonorrhoea; >35: E. coli (UTI); mumpsGradual pain, swelling, fever, dysuria, Prehn's sign (relief on elevation)
Testicular cancer15–40, cryptorchidism, FHx, KlinefelterPainless hard lump in testis, dull ache, gynaecomastia
Hydrocele / varicocele / epididymal cystTransilluminates (hydrocele, cyst: separate from testis); "bag of worms" (varicocele, usually left)
Urethral strictureInstrumentation, infection, traumaPoor flow, spraying
Erectile dysfunctionVascular (CVD marker), diabetes, drugs, neurological, psychogenic, hypogonadismAssess CV risk, HbA1c, lipids, testosterone
Bladder/renal cancer, stones, UTISee week 111Haematuria, pain

los.text: Describe the causes, pathophysiology, diagnosis and principles of treatment and management of prostate cancer
sessions: Clin 2: Prostate cancer diagnosis and management
los.html:
Epidemiology
  • Commonest cancer in UK men (~1 in 8 lifetime; 1 in 4 Black men).
  • Adenocarcinoma of the peripheral zone (palpable on DRE).
  • Risk: age, Black ethnicity, FHx, BRCA2, Lynch.
PresentationOften asymptomatic (PSA testing), LUTS (usually coincidental BPH), haematuria, erectile dysfunction, bone pain/cord compression/weight loss (metastatic).
Diagnosis
  • PSA (age-specific thresholds; raised also by BPH, prostatitis, UTI, ejaculation, vigorous exercise, catheterisation) + DRE (hard, irregular, craggy)
  • → 2WW
  • → multiparametric MRI first (Likert/PI-RADS)
  • → transperineal targeted biopsy if suspicious.
Grading/staging
  • Gleason score → ISUP grade group (1–5)
  • TNM
  • Risk groups (Cambridge Prognostic Groups CPG1–5)
  • Staging CT/bone scan or PSMA PET for higher risk.
Management
  • Low risk (CPG1–2): active surveillance (PSA, MRI, re-biopsy) to avoid overtreatment; watchful waiting if elderly/comorbid.
  • Localised intermediate/high risk: radical prostatectomy (robotic) or radical radiotherapy + androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), brachytherapy. Side effects: erectile dysfunction, urinary incontinence, bowel toxicity (RT).
  • Metastatic: ADT: LHRH agonists (goserelin; give anti-androgen cover for tumour flare) or antagonist (degarelix), orchidectomy; plus novel hormonal agents (abiraterone, enzalutamide, apalutamide, darolutamide) and/or docetaxel; bone protection, palliative RT, PARP inhibitors (BRCA).
ADT side effectsHot flushes, ↓ libido, osteoporosis, gynaecomastia, metabolic syndrome/CVD, fatigue.
ScreeningNo national programme in UK (overdiagnosis, false positives); informed choice PSA testing for men ≥50 who ask.

los.text: Describe the pathophysiology, assessment and principles of treatment and management of male lower urinary tract symptoms/benign prostatic hyperplasia
los.html:
BPH
  • Benign hyperplasia of transition zone (stromal + glandular) driven by DHT (testosterone → DHT via 5α-reductase) with ageing
  • ~50% of men by 60.
LUTSVoiding/obstructive (hesitancy, weak stream, straining, intermittency, incomplete emptying, terminal dribbling) and storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia, urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity secondary to obstruction).
Assessment
  • History
  • IPSS symptom score
  • Frequency–volume chart (nocturnal polyuria?)
  • DRE
  • Abdominal exam (palpable bladder)
  • Urine dipstick
  • U&E
  • PSA (after counselling)
  • Flow rate and post-void residual (bladder scan)
  • Urodynamics before surgery.
  • Exclude: UTI, diabetes, diuretics, nocturnal polyuria (HF, OSA), neurological bladder, prostate cancer, stricture.
Management
  • Conservative: fluid timing, ↓ caffeine/alcohol, bladder training, urethral milking.
  • α1-blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, doxazosin): relax prostatic smooth muscle → fast relief (days). SE: postural hypotension, dizziness, retrograde ejaculation, floppy iris syndrome (tell before cataract surgery).
  • 5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride): shrink prostate (~20–30%) over 6 months, ↓ retention/surgery risk; for large prostates (>30 g/PSA >1.4). SE: ↓ libido, ED, gynaecomastia; halve PSA.
  • Combination (α-blocker + 5-ARI); antimuscarinics/mirabegron for storage symptoms; PDE5i (tadalafil).
  • Surgery: TURP (SE: retrograde ejaculation, bleeding, TUR syndrome: hyponatraemia), HoLEP, Rezum/UroLift, open prostatectomy for very large glands.
Acute urinary retentionCatheterise, measure residual (>1 L → watch for post-obstructive diuresis), start tamsulosin → trial without catheter after 2–3 days.

los.text: Describe the causes, signs, symptoms, pathophysiology, diagnosis and principles of treatment / management of testicular pain and testicular cancer
sessions: Clin 4: Testicular pain and testicular cancer
los.html:
Testicular torsion
  • Twisting of spermatic cord → venous then arterial occlusion.
  • Peak 12–18 yrs (and neonates).
  • Sudden severe unilateral pain ± abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex, negative Prehn's.
  • Surgical emergency: exploration within 6 hours (salvage ~90% → falls rapidly) + bilateral orchidopexy.
  • Don't delay for imaging.
Other causes of pain
  • Torsion of testicular appendage (hydatid of Morgagni: "blue dot sign", conservative)
  • Epididymo-orchitis (STI screen: NAAT; ceftriaxone + doxycycline if STI likely; ofloxacin/levofloxacin or co-amoxiclav if enteric)
  • Trauma
  • Mumps orchitis
  • Referred pain (renal colic, inguinal hernia, AAA).
Testicular cancer
  • Commonest solid cancer in men 15–40. Risk factors: cryptorchidism (×4–10; even after orchidopexy), previous testicular cancer, FHx, Klinefelter, subfertility, HIV.
  • Germ cell tumours (~95%): seminoma (30–40 yrs; radiosensitive; PLAP, mild ↑ hCG) and non-seminomatous (teratoma, embryonal, yolk sac (AFP), choriocarcinoma (hCG); 20–30 yrs). Precursor GCNIS.
  • Presentation: painless hard lump, heaviness, ± hydrocele, gynaecomastia (hCG), back pain (para-aortic nodes), breathlessness (lung mets).
  • Ix: scrotal USS, tumour markers (AFP, β-hCG, LDH), CT chest/abdomen/pelvis.
  • Rx: radical inguinal orchidectomy (not scrotal approach: preserves lymphatic drainage), offer sperm banking and prosthesis; surveillance, chemotherapy (BEP: bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin) or radiotherapy depending on stage. Cure rate >95%.
  • Lymphatic drainage to para-aortic nodes (testis descended from abdomen); scrotal skin → inguinal nodes.

los.text: Explain how ultrasound and other imaging techniques can be used to identify testicular diseases
los.html:
• Scrotal ultrasound (with Doppler) is first-line for scrotal swelling/pain: high-frequency linear probe; no radiation.
FindingUltrasound features
Testicular tumourIntratesticular solid mass, usually hypoechoic; seminoma homogeneous, NSGCT heterogeneous with cystic areas/calcification; ↑ vascularity
TorsionAbsent/reduced Doppler flow, enlarged heterogeneous testis, "whirlpool sign" of twisted cord. (Clinical diagnosis takes priority: don't delay surgery)
Epididymo-orchitisEnlarged epididymis/testis with ↑ blood flow (hyperaemia), reactive hydrocele, abscess
HydroceleAnechoic fluid surrounding testis (check underlying testis!)
Epididymal cyst/spermatoceleAnechoic cyst in epididymis, separate from testis
VaricoceleDilated veins >3 mm in pampiniform plexus, reflux on Valsalva (new right-sided or non-reducing → image kidney: renal tumour)
MicrolithiasisMultiple tiny echogenic foci (association with GCNIS debated)
TraumaRupture (tunica albuginea disruption), haematoma
Other imaging
  • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging testicular cancer (para-aortic nodes, lung mets)
  • MRI for indeterminate lesions or locating undescended testes
  • Tumour markers complement imaging
  • USS also guides varicocele embolisation.
Key pointAn intratesticular solid mass is malignant until proven otherwise; most extratesticular lesions are benign.

los.text: Describe the pathogenesis of prevalent testicular and prostate disorders
sessions: Path: Pathogenesis of common testicular and prostate disorders
los.html:
BPH
  • Age-related ↑ DHT (5α-reductase type 2 in stromal cells) and oestrogen:androgen ratio
  • → growth factors (FGF, TGF-β)
  • → nodular hyperplasia of glands and stroma in the transition and periurethral zones
  • → urethral compression
  • ↑ smooth muscle tone (α1).
  • Not premalignant.
Prostate cancer
  • Peripheral zone adenocarcinoma.
  • Precursor high-grade PIN.
  • Androgen-dependent growth (AR signalling)
  • TMPRSS2–ERG fusion (~50%), PTEN loss, BRCA2, MYC, TP53 in advanced disease
  • Castration resistance via AR amplification/splice variants (AR-V7).
  • Histology: small crowded glands, loss of basal cell layer (p63/HMWCK negative), prominent nucleoli, perineural invasion
  • Gleason pattern (architecture).
  • Spreads locally (seminal vesicles, bladder) and to bone (osteosclerotic metastases) via Batson's venous plexus, lymph nodes.
ProstatitisAscending infection (E. coli), reflux of urine into ducts; chronic pelvic pain syndrome multifactorial.
Testicular germ cell tumours
  • Arise from GCNIS (fetal germ cells failing to mature) linked to testicular dysgenesis (cryptorchidism, hypospadias, subfertility)
  • Isochromosome 12p (i(12p)) almost universal
  • KIT mutations in seminoma.
  • Seminoma: sheets of large clear cells with lymphocytes.
  • Teratoma: tissues of different germ layers.
TorsionCongenital bell-clapper deformity (high tunica vaginalis insertion) allows the testis to rotate → venous congestion → haemorrhagic infarction.
Epididymo-orchitisAscending infection from urethra/bladder; mumps via haematogenous spread → atrophy/infertility.
HydrocelePatent processus vaginalis (infants) or imbalance of secretion/absorption of tunica vaginalis (adults; secondary to tumour, infection, trauma).

los.text: Describe the structure and function of the male human reproductive system and summarise spermatogenesis
los.html:
Anatomy
  • Testes (in scrotum ~2–3 °C below core temperature: pampiniform plexus counter-current cooling, dartos and cremaster muscles)
  • Epididymis (head, body, tail: sperm maturation and storage ~2 weeks)
  • Vas deferens (in spermatic cord through inguinal canal → ampulla)
  • Seminal vesicles (~60–70% of semen: fructose, prostaglandins, fibrinogen; alkaline)
  • Ejaculatory ducts → prostate (~20–30%: PSA (liquefies semen), zinc, citrate)
  • Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands (pre-ejaculate mucus)
  • Urethra (prostatic, membranous, spongy)
  • Penis (corpora cavernosa + corpus spongiosum).
Testis structureTunica albuginea → lobules of seminiferous tubules (spermatogenesis; Sertoli cells) with Leydig cells in the interstitium.
Hormonal control (HPG axis)
  • Pulsatile GnRH → LH → Leydig cells → testosterone
  • FSH → Sertoli cells (+ high intratesticular testosterone) → spermatogenesis, ABP (androgen-binding protein), inhibin (negative feedback on FSH).
  • Testosterone negatively feeds back on LH/GnRH
  • Converted to DHT (prostate, external genitalia, hair) and oestradiol.
Spermatogenesis (~64–74 days)
  • Spermatogonia (mitosis; stem cells at basement membrane)
  • → primary spermatocytes (46, meiosis I)
  • → secondary spermatocytes (23)
  • → meiosis II
  • → spermatids
  • → spermiogenesis (acrosome, flagellum, nuclear condensation, cytoplasm shed)
  • → spermatozoa
  • → released into lumen
  • → epididymis (gain motility and capacitation in female tract).
  • Sertoli cells form the blood–testis barrier (tight junctions) protecting germ cells from immune attack.
Erection
  • Parasympathetic (S2–4) → NO → cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation → engorgement (PDE5 inhibitors prolong).
  • Emission/ejaculation: sympathetic (T12–L2) + somatic (pudendal) ("Point and Shoot").
Normal semen (WHO)Volume ≥1.4 mL, concentration ≥16 million/mL, total motility ≥42%, normal forms ≥4%.

los.text: Explain the social factors influencing men's health and how they relate to testicular and prostate disease
los.html:
Men's health outcomes (UK)
  • Life expectancy ~4 years shorter than women
  • Higher rates of premature CVD, cancer deaths, suicide (~¾ of suicides), alcohol and drug deaths, accidents/violence, workplace injury
  • Men use primary care less and present later.
Social factors
  • Masculinity norms ("hegemonic masculinity", Connell): stoicism, self-reliance, risk-taking, reluctance to show vulnerability → delayed help-seeking, under-reporting of symptoms (urinary symptoms, testicular lumps, depression), embarrassment about genital/sexual problems.
  • Socioeconomic position: manual occupations, unemployment, low income; access issues (GP opening hours conflicting with work).
  • Health literacy and awareness: low awareness of testicular self-examination and prostate cancer risk (especially in Black men: 1 in 4 lifetime risk).
  • Ethnicity and culture: stigma, mistrust, language.
  • Service design: services perceived as "female-oriented"; fewer routine touch points (no equivalent of cervical screening/contraception visits).
Testicular and prostate disease
  • Testicular cancer affects young men who rarely see doctors (embarrassment, "it's nothing") → delayed presentation
  • Prostate symptoms seen as normal ageing
  • Erectile dysfunction rarely raised though it is a CVD marker
  • Fear of treatment side effects (incontinence, impotence) affects decisions.
Interventions
  • Awareness campaigns (Movember, Prostate Cancer UK, "Check your balls")
  • Workplace and community outreach (barbershops, football clubs, Men's Sheds)
  • Flexible/online access
  • Normalising conversations
  • Male-friendly framing (practical, action-oriented)
  • Opportunistic checks.
